Sexual dimorphism in body mass is a notable feature of Nyctyornis athertoni, with males consistently attaining a greater asymptotic body mass than females. The maximum adult body mass recorded for females reaches approximately 82.25 grams [Wwi = approximately 82.25 grams], representing the ultimate wet weight for females, whereas males can achieve an ultimate wet weight of up to 89 grams [Wwi = up to 89 grams]. The relatively larger male mass may also confer advantages in territorial defense and mate acquisition, behaviors that are energetically costly. These size values place the species at the larger end of the body-size spectrum within the Meropidae, correlating with its ability to hunt larger hymenopteran prey.

Following fledging, the juvenile birds remain dependent on their parents for provisioning for several additional weeks, during which they refine their hunting skills. The attainment of sexual maturity, or puberty, is a considerably slower process. Under the same thermal regime, the time since birth at puberty is 105 days [tp = 105 days], a duration that allows for the full development of the characteristic plumage and the complex foraging apparatus required for capturing bees and wasps.
